# Data & Basic Analysis

## Data Verification

It's always a good idea to make sure the data are input and interpreted properly. *Mea culpa*. I forgot to do this. So, this step was actually slipped in later in the analysis stream but is presented here as this is a more logical location.

```{r}
# Load necessary libraries
if (!require("gt")) install.packages("gt")
if (!require("dplyr")) install.packages("dplyr")
if (!require("tidyr")) install.packages("tidyr")
if (!require("glue")) install.packages("glue")

library(gt)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(glue)

# 1. Define Helper Function for Text Color
get_text_color <- function(hex) {
  if (is.na(hex)) return("black") 
  rgb <- col2rgb(hex)
  lum <- (0.299 * rgb[1] + 0.587 * rgb[2] + 0.114 * rgb[3]) / 255
  if (lum > 0.5) return("black") else return("white")
}

# 2. Define the Cell Formatting Function (Scalar Version)
fmt_color_cell_worker <- function(name, hex) {
  # Handle NAs (Blank Cells)
  if (is.na(name) || is.na(hex)) {
    return("<div style='background-color: white; width: 100%; height: 100%;'></div>")
  }
  
  # Determine text color based on background
  text_col <- get_text_color(hex)
  
  # Return HTML
  glue(
    "<div style='
      background-color: {hex}; 
      color: {text_col}; 
      width: 100%; 
      height: 100%; 
      padding: 8px; 
      border-radius: 4px;
      font-weight: bold;
      text-align: center;
      font-size: 12px;'>
      {name}
    </div>"
  )
}

# 3. Vectorize the Function
fmt_color_cell <- Vectorize(fmt_color_cell_worker)

# 4. Create the Data (Historically Accurate)
data_raw <- tribble(
  ~Year, ~Pantone_Name, ~Pantone_Hex, ~BM_Name, ~BM_Hex, ~SW_Name, ~SW_Hex, ~Akzo_Name, ~Akzo_Hex, ~Glid_Name, ~Glid_Hex, ~Dunn_Name, ~Dunn_Hex, ~Behr_Name, ~Behr_Hex, ~Val_Name, ~Val_Hex,

# 5. Process the DataFrame
df_formatted <- data_raw %>%
  mutate(
    Pantone = fmt_color_cell(Pantone_Name, Pantone_Hex),
    Benjamin_Moore = fmt_color_cell(BM_Name, BM_Hex),
    Sherwin_Williams = fmt_color_cell(SW_Name, SW_Hex),
    AkzoNobel = fmt_color_cell(Akzo_Name, Akzo_Hex),
    Glidden = fmt_color_cell(Glid_Name, Glid_Hex),
    Dunn_Edwards = fmt_color_cell(Dunn_Name, Dunn_Hex),
    Behr = fmt_color_cell(Behr_Name, Behr_Hex),
    Valspar = fmt_color_cell(Val_Name, Val_Hex)
  ) %>%
  select(Year, Pantone, Benjamin_Moore, Sherwin_Williams, AkzoNobel, Glidden, Dunn_Edwards, Behr, Valspar)

# 6. Handle Split Years (The Fix)
# Instead of complex HTML, we use standard cells with "multi-color" and white background
df_formatted$Pantone[df_formatted$Year == 2021] <- fmt_color_cell("multi-color", "#FFFFFF")
df_formatted$Pantone[df_formatted$Year == 2016] <- fmt_color_cell("multi-color", "#FFFFFF")

# 7. Generate Table
gt_table <- df_formatted %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_markdown(columns = everything()) %>%
  cols_label(
    Year = "Year",
    Pantone = "Pantone",
    Benjamin_Moore = "Benj. Moore",
    Sherwin_Williams = "Sherwin-W.",
    AkzoNobel = "AkzoNobel",
    Glidden = "Glidden",
    Dunn_Edwards = "Dunn-Edw.",
    Behr = "Behr",
    Valspar = "Valspar"
  ) %>%
  tab_header(
    title = md("**The Spectrum of Choice (2016–2026)**"),
    subtitle = "Color of the Year selections (Blank cells indicate no single COTY selected)"
  ) %>%
  cols_width(
    Year ~ px(50),
    everything() ~ px(100)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = list(cell_fill(color = "#f4f4f4"), cell_text(weight = "bold")),
    locations = cells_body(columns = Year)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = list(cell_text(weight = "bold", size = "large")),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  )

# Print
gt_table
```

As explained earlier, the margins of this image were removed so that the names of the companies weren't in the image. The AI engine was pretty good at guessing the companies. I helped to make sure that were all correct.

## General Analysis

The AI engine responded to the question that I phrased earlier regarding generalizations about colors and whether there are any trends in the choices. Here is the response.

Based on the chart provided and current design trends for 2026, we can identify several distinct generalizations and shifts in color philosophy over the last decade.

The columns in your chart correspond to major color authorities. By cross-referencing the specific colors (like the 2016 and 2021 "split" swatches and the 2026 selections), we can identify the key players:

-   **Column 1:** **Pantone** (Famous for the split "Rose Quartz/Serenity" in 2016 and "Ultimate Gray/Illuminating" in 2021).

-   **Column 2:** **Benjamin Moore** (Note the shift to "Silhouette" dark charcoal/brown in 2026).

-   **Column 3:** **Sherwin-Williams** (Note the "Universal Khaki" in 2026).

-   **Columns 4–8:** Other major paint brands: **AkzoNobel, Glidden, Dunn Edwards, Behr, and Valspar**. (This is edited to reflect the information that I gave the AI engine)

Here are the generalizations and trends visible in the table:

### 1. The "Mood" Timeline

The colors serve as a timeline of the global emotional state (the *zeitgeist*):

-   **2015–2019 (The Exploration Era):** The colors were experimental and varied. We see bold purples (Ultra Violet, 2018), vibrant corals (Living Coral, 2019), and spicy reds.

-   **2020–2021 (The Crisis & Safety Era):** As the pandemic hit, the colors shifted dramatically to "safety" colors. Blue (classic, calm, stable) dominates 2020. 2021 introduces Grey (resilience) and Yellow (hope).

-   **2022–2024 (The Healing & Nesting Era):** Post-pandemic, the trend moved to "biophilic" colors—tones that mimic nature to make homes feel restorative. This is the era of sage greens (2022) and warm, fuzzy peaches/terracottas (2023–2024).

-   **2025–2026 (The "New Foundations" Era):** The most recent rows show a distinct shift away from pastels toward **Deep Moody Tones** (charcoal, dark chocolate) and **Blank Slates** (White).

### 2. 2026 is the Year of the "Reset"

The top row (2026) shows a fascinating divergence between "High Fashion" and "Home Decor":

-   **The "Clean Slate":** Pantone (Column 1) selected **Cloud Dancer (White)**. After years of bold colors, this signals a desire to wipe the slate clean and start fresh—a "silence" amidst the noise.

-   **The "Grounding":** In contrast, the paint brands (Cols 2 & 3) chose **Deep Browns and Khakis** (e.g., Benjamin Moore's *Silhouette* and Sherwin-Williams' *Universal Khaki*). This suggests that for interiors, people want stability and earthiness rather than stark minimalism.

### 3. Green is the "New Neutral"

If you look at the right half of the chart (Columns 6, 7, 8), you will see a massive amount of **Green** appearing consistently, especially in 2022 and 2026.

-   While Grey used to be the default neutral (see 2016–2019), **Green** has replaced it.

-   In 2026 specifically, while the big names went White/Brown, the consumer brands (Behr, Valspar, Glidden) all selected variations of **Jade, Eucalyptus, and Olive**. This generalization holds true: *When in doubt, the paint industry bets on Green.*

### 4. The "Split" Anomaly

The chart highlights two unique instances in Column 1 (Pantone) where two colors were chosen instead of one:

-   **2016 (Rose Quartz & Serenity):** A soft pink and blue. This was a commentary on gender fluidity and mindfulness.

-   **2021 (Illuminating & Ultimate Gray):** A bright yellow and solid grey. This represented "light at the end of the tunnel" (Yellow) supported by fortitude (Grey) during the pandemic recovery.

### Summary Table of Eras

|               |                    |                                      |
|---------------|--------------------|--------------------------------------|
| **Era**       | **Dominant Vibe**  | **Key Colors**                       |
| **Pre-2020**  | Bold, Expressive   | Ultra Violet, Living Coral, Greenery |
| **2020-2021** | Safety, Resilience | Classic Blue, Ultimate Gray, Naval   |
| **2022-2024** | Comfort, Nature    | Peach Fuzz, Sage Green, Terra Cotta  |
| **2025-2026** | Grounding, Reset   | White, Dark Brown, Khaki, Deep Jade  |
